Maladaptive Strategies.value: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
Making eye contact with other people
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner in this 34-year-old male unless there is unreported trauma content involving pregnancy, childbirth, or infants. The other trigger items point toward sexualized/interpersonal threat and hospital-associated reminders, making this item the clearest trauma-incongruent outlier.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeated lock-checking is more suggestive of fear of external intrusion/burglary than trauma-specific coping with partner physical abuse, and it is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The other maladaptive strategies reflect interpersonal avoidance and affect suppression, whereas this item introduces a different safety concern.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item duplicates compulsive checking behavior rather than describing a perceived current threat state, and it implies fear of break-in/external danger that is not otherwise supported by the trauma narrative, appraisals, or memory content. In combination with the matching maladaptive strategy item, it forms an internally coherent pair but one that is poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

vignette:
Kofi remembers the night it ended not as a single event, but as a series of sensory fragments that refuse to stay in the past. It began with the look in his ex-partner's eyes-a possessive, appraising stare that made Kofi feel less like a person and more like an object to be controlled. The argument that followed is a blur, but he can still hear his partner's voice, a low, menacing whisper repeating the same phrase over and over, an auditory loop that plays in his head without warning. He remembers the sharp, metallic taste of blood filling his mouth after his lip split against the floor. And he remembers the sterile, chemical smell of the emergency room where he spent the next six hours, a scent that now seems to cling to every corner of his life. That was nine months ago.

In the time since, the world has become a landscape of potential threats. As a parole officer, Kofi's job requires him to sit in small, enclosed rooms with men, many of whom have a history of violence. He used to pride himself on his ability to connect, to be firm but fair. Now, every client interview is an exercise in terror. He finds himself unable to meet their eyes, his gaze fixed on a spot on the wall just over their shoulder. He feels his body lock up, his shoulders bunching around his ears, a posture of constant readiness for an attack that never comes. He watches their hands, their shifting weight, the subtle changes in their expression, certain that he is moments away from having to defend himself. He knows, logically, that he is safe, but the feeling of being alone with a man in a closed space is suffocating. He has started letting minor infractions slide, avoiding the necessary confrontations of his job simply because the thought of any disagreement, however small, sends a jolt of panic through him. His supervisor recently noted his "decreased engagement" in his performance review.

The memories are not like memories at all; they feel like visitations. Last week, a janitor used an antiseptic cleaner on a countertop in the office breakroom. The smell hit Kofi instantly, and he was no longer in his workplace. He was back on the cold floor of his old apartment, the taste of blood sharp on his tongue, his ex-partner's whispered words echoing in his ears as if he were standing right beside him. The memory was so vivid, so present, that he flinched, dropping his coffee mug, which shattered on the tile. He stood frozen, his heart hammering, until a colleague asked if he was alright. He couldn't explain that for a full thirty seconds, he had not been there at all.

This pervasive sense of threat has poisoned every part of his life. He is in a new relationship with a kind, patient woman, but he finds himself pushing her away. When she shows him affection or when a moment of genuine happiness begins to surface, a cold dread washes over him. Joy feels like a trap, a dangerous vulnerability he cannot afford. He has come to believe that his life was irrevocably broken that night. The injustice of it is a constant, bitter pill; his ex-partner faced no consequences, while Kofi feels he is serving a life sentence. He sees his career faltering, his new relationship strained by a distance he creates but cannot seem to dismantle. He feels hollowed out. It was this creeping, persistent thought-that perhaps his life was no longer worth the exhausting effort of living it-that finally propelled him to seek help. He came to therapy not with a clear hope, but with a desperate fear that the man he was before the trauma is gone for good.
